top.title: Music can enhance the flavor of your food
top.summary: The moment we take a sip of our morning coffee or our first bite of lunch, the brain begins interpreting what we taste. Is it sweet? Sour? Or something else entirely? But the brain does not create flavor based solely on signals from the tongue. That is the finding of a new study from the Department of Food Science, published in Scientific Reports.

top.title: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger
top.summary: Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.
top.text: Stress does more than influence how we feel. It can also change what we remember, particularly when an experience is emotionally intense or personally meaningful. Scientists have long known that cortisol, a hormone released during stressful situations, can strengthen emotional memories. What has been less clear is exactly how this happens inside the brain. Researchers at Yale University have now uncovered important clues. Their study reveals that cortisol strengthens emotional memories by changing how brain networks involved in emotion and memory function and communicate with one another. The findings offer a deeper understanding of why certain experiences leave such powerful impressions while others quickly fade. "We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," said corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences. The findings were published in the journal Science Advances . Previous research involving both humans and rodents has shown that stress and cortisol can improve memory for emotional events. Scientists also know that certain brain regions, including the amygdala, play an essential role in this process. The amygdala is particularly important for processing emotions and identifying experiences that may be significant. However, understanding precisely how cortisol strengthens memories has been challenging. Many brain regions participate in several mental functions, making it difficult to determine whether the hormone is influencing emotional responses, memory formation, or both. "Forming memories for emotional experiences involves different processes in the brain: first, perceiving an experience as emotional or intense, and second, encoding that experience into long-term memory," said Goldfarb, who is also a member of Yale's Wu Tsai Institute, an interdisciplinary research initiative that explores cognition. The researchers wanted to examine these processes separately to determine how cortisol affects the brain's ability to recognize emotional significance and preserve an experience as a lasting memory. To investigate, the Yale team conducted an experiment in which participants took a pill containing either hydrocortisone, a form of cortisol, or an inactive placebo. They then viewed a series of pictures while undergoing functional MRI (fMRI) scanning. This imaging technique measures changes in blood flow and oxygen levels associated with brain activity, allowing researchers to identify which areas of the brain are more active during different tasks. As participants examined the pictures, they reported their emotional reactions to each image. The following day, researchers tested how well they remembered what they had seen. Each person completed the experiment twice, once after receiving hydrocortisone and once after receiving the placebo. The study used a double blind design, meaning neither the participants nor the experimenter knew which substance had been administered during a particular session. This approach allowed the scientists to compare how the same person's brain responded with and without the additional cortisol. One of the study's most important advances came from the way researchers analyzed the brain scans. Scientists often study a measurement called functional connectivity, which describes how closely activity in different parts of the brain fluctuates together. When two regions show synchronized patterns of activity, it can indicate that they are participating in related processes. Traditionally, examining these relationships requires several minutes of brain imaging data. The Yale team instead analyzed functional connectivity during individual trials lasting only around five seconds. Using these brief snapshots, the researchers tested whether patterns of brain activity could predict two different outcomes: how emotionally intense participants found a picture and whether they would remember that picture the following day. The approach worked for both. By identifying patterns associated with emotional intensity and memory formation separately, the scientists were able to examine how cortisol influenced each network and the interactions between them. This gave the researchers a more detailed picture of the changing brain activity associated with emotional memory formation. First, cortisol improved participants' ability to remember emotionally significant experiences, confirming what earlier research had suggested. Second, and more importantly, the hormone strengthened emotional memory through distinct changes in the brain networks responsible for processing emotion and forming memories. In networks associated with emotion, cortisol produced more consistent patterns of activity and increased their engagement. This suggests that the hormone helped the brain respond more strongly and reliably to the emotional significance of an experience. In memory networks, cortisol had a different effect. It made their activity patterns more specialized for emotional information, suggesting that the brain was adjusting how it encoded emotionally meaningful experiences. The hormone also increased coordination between the networks involved in emotion and memory. In other words, cortisol appeared to help these different brain systems work together more effectively when processing experiences that carried emotional weight. Together, these findings suggest that stress strengthens emotional memories through several interacting brain mechanisms rather than through a single region or process. The results help explain why stress does not necessarily improve memory for everything. Instead, its benefits appear to be selective, making experiences that feel particularly intense or meaningful more likely to be remembered. The researchers believe this reflects the brain's ability to adapt to stressful situations by prioritizing information that may be important. "Stress responses are fundamentally adaptive and can help you form strong memories -- but this is specific to experiences that you find to be emotionally intense or meaningful," Goldfarb said. "This is in part related to your brain increasing engagement of networks that track emotional intensity. So, if you are stressed out and trying to learn something new, it might help to think about exciting elements or strong feelings connected to what you are learning." The findings also point to a potentially useful insight about learning. Connecting information to something exciting, personally important, or emotionally engaging could make it easier to remember, particularly during stressful situations. Rather than simply disrupting memory, stress can sometimes help the brain identify which experiences deserve special attention and strengthen the networks involved in preserving them. Other Yale researchers involved in the study include Rajita Sinha, the Foundations Fund Endowed Professor in Psychiatry and professor in the Child Study Center and of neuroscience at Yale School of Medicine (YSM), and Todd Constable, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson Professor of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging and professor of neurosurgery at YSM. top.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
top.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.
top.text: Plastic pollution is one of the world's most persistent environmental problems. Vast amounts of discarded plastic accumulate in the oceans, sometimes forming enormous garbage patches that threaten marine life. Most conventional plastics break down extremely slowly because microorganisms struggle to digest the synthetic polymers from which they are made. Instead of disappearing, these materials gradually fragment into increasingly smaller particles, including microplastics and nanoplastics. Yet plastic waste is not completely beyond the reach of nature. Bacteria and other microorganisms can colonize its surfaces, forming communities known as biofilms. These communities create a distinctive microbial ecosystem that scientists call the "plastisphere." Researchers at the University of Konstanz have now discovered an unusual enzyme that could reveal how some bacteria are becoming better equipped to break down certain types of plastic. The enzyme can digest particular polyesters and biodegradable plastics, but it has another unexpected ability: it can also break down penicillin, suggesting a possible connection to antibiotic resistance. Scientists have nicknamed it the "Pac-Man enzyme" because its molecular structure features a remarkably wide opening where chemical reactions take place, known as the active site. The discovery suggests that bacteria may be adapting to digest certain plastic materials more quickly than researchers previously believed. However, the findings also highlight an important limitation. For microorganisms to make a meaningful difference in reducing plastic pollution, more plastic products would need to be made from biodegradable materials that contain chemical bonds microbes can break apart. To investigate how microorganisms digest biodegradable plastics, University of Konstanz biologists Harry Lerner and David Schleheck studied the entire process of microbial decomposition. They wanted to determine not only whether the materials could be completely broken down, but also which microorganisms were responsible and what biological mechanisms allowed them to do it. The researchers examined the composition of the microbial communities involved and analyzed their collective genetic information (the metagenome). This approach allowed them to search for genes that might produce enzymes capable of breaking apart plastic polymers. Their experiments focused on long-chain aliphatic polyesters (LCAP), a class of biodegradable plastic materials developed by a research team led by chemist Stefan Mecking. These materials contain chemical bonds that certain microorganisms can potentially break down, unlike the more resistant structures found in many conventional plastics. The collaborative findings were published in The ISME Journal . To observe how the bioplastics behaved in a natural environment, the team placed samples beneath the surface of forest soil at the university's botanical garden. "We buried small pieces of LCAP bioplastic film in the upper humus layer in the forest at the university's botanical garden, about ten centimeters deep," explains Harry Lerner. "This layer is where the breakdown of cellulose and other natural polymers, such as cutin - a plant-based polyester - takes place." Humus is the upper layer of soil rich in decomposing organic matter, where microorganisms play a major role in recycling nutrients. Cellulose is the main structural component of plant cell walls, while cutin is a naturally occurring polyester that helps form the protective outer covering of plants. The researchers selected this environment because its microorganisms already possess the biological machinery needed to break down complex natural materials. Alongside the outdoor experiment, the scientists carried out laboratory tests using soil collected from the same forest. They mixed powdered bioplastics into the soil and monitored microbial activity over the course of an entire year. One important measurement was the amount of carbon dioxide, or CO2, released from the samples. As microorganisms consume and metabolize organic materials, they produce carbon dioxide through respiration. Tracking this gas helped the researchers determine how actively the microbes were breaking down the plastics. The buried plastic films remained in the forest soil for a full year, allowing the team to compare decomposition under natural conditions with the carefully monitored laboratory experiments. To assess the results, the scientists also tested cellulose, other biodegradable plastics, conventional polyethylene plastic, and soil samples without added materials. "Cellulose, other types of bioplastics such as PHBV and PCL, as well as high-density plastic (HDPE) and untreated soil were used as controls in the laboratory. We found that all bioplastic materials were completely degraded within roughly 250 to 330 days. Cellulose broke down after about 80 days, whereas virtually no degradation occurred for HDPE," says Lerner. The difference was striking. While the biodegradable plastics were completely broken down within approximately nine to eleven months, conventional high-density polyethylene showed almost no decomposition. These results demonstrate why the chemical makeup of plastic matters so much. Some polymers contain bonds that microbial enzymes can attack, allowing bacteria to dismantle them into smaller molecules. Others, including widely used polyethylene, are far more resistant to biological degradation. When the researchers recovered the plastic films from the forest soil, they discovered something unexpected. Using electron microscopy, which can reveal structures far too small to see with an ordinary light microscope, the team examined the surfaces of the buried materials. They found numerous tiny holes, each approximately matching the dimensions and shape of an individual bacterial cell. The unusual pattern suggested that bacteria were doing more than simply attaching themselves to the plastic. They appeared to be breaking into the material itself. "We hypothesized that bacteria are coated with plastic-depolymerases anchored to their cell surfaces. This would enable them to digest their way into the material and become embedded within the film, leaving behind microscopic holes of exactly this type," explains Lerner. Depolymerases are enzymes that break large molecules called polymers into smaller chemical units. If these enzymes are attached directly to the outside of a bacterium, they could allow the microorganism to digest the surrounding material while remaining in close contact with it. This would help explain the microscopic cavities observed in the plastic films. Rather than relying entirely on enzymes released into the environment, the bacteria might be able to break down the material directly at their surfaces. To find the biological machinery behind this unusual behavior, Lerner extracted DNA from the entire community of microorganisms living in the soil samples. He then sequenced the genetic material and carefully analyzed the extensive data to determine which microbes and genes became especially abundant as the bioplastics decomposed. One gene stood out. It was strongly enriched specifically in forest soil containing LCAP, suggesting that it could play an important role in breaking down the biodegradable polyester. Further analysis revealed that the gene produces an esterase, a type of enzyme capable of splitting certain chemical bonds found in esters. These bonds are present in many naturally occurring substances as well as in various biodegradable polyesters. What made this particular enzyme especially interesting was how it was positioned on bacterial cells. top.title: Hypnosis may help relieve stomach pain
top.summary: Stomach pain and other gastrointestinal complaints are common among children and adolescents. When symptoms recur over a long period, the cause may be a form of DGBI (disorders of gut-brain interaction), in which communication between the brain and the gut does not function as it should. This can affect both intestinal motility and the way pain is perceived.

top.title: First drug-focused guideline outlines newer treatments for primary biliary cholangitis
top.summary: For the first time, a joint guideline from the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) and American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) evaluates newer medications for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), the most common cholestatic disease in adults. Published in Gastroenterology and HEPATOLOGY, the guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis and treatment.

top.title: For centuries, bird migration was a mystery – a tech revolution is changing that, and could help save these amazing creatures
top.summary: An early clue came from storks found in Europe with African arrows in their bodies. Today, an atlas reveals hundreds of bird migration routes that are both complicated and remarkable.
top.text: For more than 2,000 years , scientists have scratched their heads over one of the most basic mysteries of the natural world: Where do birds go? Billions of birds appear and disappear with the seasons every year. Early naturalists offered explanations for the disappearances that today seem fantastical: Birds transformed into other species , one theory went. Others suggested they hibernated underwater or even migrated to the moon . The truth, that these small animals were traveling thousands of miles across the planet, must once have seemed just as improbable. Then, in the early 1800s, dramatic evidence emerged supporting the theory of migration. White storks began appearing in Germany with African arrows embedded in their bodies. These birds became known as pfeilstörche , or “arrow storks .” They provided compelling evidence that birds disappearing from Europe were traveling all the way to Africa and back. Almost two centuries later, scientists are still asking the same question, but our ability to answer it has been transformed. For most of ornithological history, scientists understood migration through brief glimpses of a bird, a specimen collected somewhere else, or the rare instance of a banded bird recovered hundreds or thousands of miles from where it had been marked. From these fragments of intelligence, scientists reconstructed journeys that took place largely beyond their view. Today, it’s possible to see the journeys themselves, almost in real time. Bird banding was the first tool used to attempt a systematic approach to connect these fragments of information. Since the early 1900s, researchers have placed uniquely numbered metal bands on birds and hoped someone, somewhere, would encounter them again. Of more than 79 million birds banded, only about 6.5 million have been recovered . That generally told scientists just two things: where a bird was banded and where it was encountered again. Everything between them remained invisible. Over the past quarter-century or so, the tools used to determine where birds go have changed dramatically. Tracking devices can now be carried by increasingly smaller birds, recording their movements and communicating with land-based receivers or satellites orbiting the earth. Testing stable isotopes in feathers and other tissues can reveal where a bird originated. Genetic testing can distinguish populations. At the same time, the extraordinary growth of bird-watching and citizen science has created another revolution. Millions of observations by bird-watchers submitted to eBird , an online database to record the birds they see, show the distribution and abundance of birds across a continent throughout the year in ways early ornithologists could scarcely have imagined. Collectively, these methods open an extraordinary new window into migratory birds and one of nature’s most remarkable behaviors: migration. More than 70% of North American bird species are migratory. Yet scientists have known surprisingly little about where specific populations go. A species like the American robin may breed across thousands of miles of North America, with different breeding populations migrating to entirely different places for the winter. Birds breeding in one part of the continent may travel one route and encounter one set of environmental conditions, while members of the same species experience a completely different set of conditions along another route. These connections between where a bird breeds and where it spends the winter is called migratory connectivity . They are critical for understanding everything from the consequences of climate change on birds to how avian pathogens and diseases spread, to a species’ basic ecology. We are ornithologists and conservation scientists who have spent almost 15 years along with a team of contributors compiling this rapidly expanding knowledge on bird movement into The Atlas of North America’s Migratory Birds . It is being published Nov. 3, 2026, by Princeton University Press, with all profits going to bird conservation and research in Latin America and the Caribbean. The atlas covers the latest information on seasonal movements for nearly 600 species and combines a century of bird-banding data with eBird observations, tracking studies, stable isotope testing, genetics and other sources of information. What emerges is a picture of migratory birds that is both more complicated and more remarkable than the simple arrows pointing between breeding and wintering ranges on a map. Consider the yellow-billed cuckoo . These birds breed over a wide range of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. but migrate to a relatively small wintering area in the Gran Chaco region of northern Argentina, Paraguay and southern Bolivia. In contrast, peregrine falcons that breed in Alaska migrate almost directly south, dispersing across the Americas to wintering grounds that extend as far as southern South America. Discoveries like these are accumulating rapidly. Collectively, they amount to a renaissance in our understanding of animal movement never before imagined. The more clearly scientists can follow individual birds and populations across the planet, the more extraordinary these species can seem. Migratory birds such as the arctic tern and northern wheatear cross oceans, deserts and mountain ranges. Some, like the bar-tailed godwits, fly thousands of miles without stopping . Others, like the American redstart, return year after year to remarkably precise breeding and wintering locations. They navigate landscapes and respond to winds, weather, food and environmental conditions across enormous geographic scales. We see these species and their migrations as among evolution’s great living masterpieces. That’s why we combined science with natural history and artist John Anderton’s extraordinary illustrations of the birds themselves. The maps allow us to see where birds travel, and the art brings the species to life. Together, they make visible something that humans could only imagine for most of our history. North America has lost about 3 billion birds during the past half-century, and many migratory species continue to decline. To understand why a population is declining and help save it, researchers need to understand the species’ entire annual cycle: its critical stopover habitats, wintering grounds and threats along its migration routes. For much of the history of ornithology, scientists studied birds primarily during their breeding season. That made practical sense. Birds are conspicuous then – singing, defending territories, building nests and raising young. But a migratory bird may spend only a few months of its life in its breeding grounds. Conditions such as weather, food availability and habitat quality encountered during migration can determine whether an individual survives to breed again . Drought thousands of miles away can affect a bird’s condition months later. American redstarts depart later after dry winters and produce fewer young . Declining horseshoe crab populations in Delaware Bay have reduced food availability for migrating red knots , contributing to lower survival . All of this knowledge has accumulated because people value birds and have devoted enormous time and effort to understanding them. For more than a century, thousands of bird-banders have woken up before the crack of dawn to set traps, carefully place bands on birds’ legs and release them, often knowing the chances of ever learning what happened to those individuals were exceedingly small. More recently, tracking technology has allowed researchers to follow individual birds across continents and oceans . Those tracks exist because scientists, students, technicians and others have spent countless hours attaching and recovering tags, and contributing and sharing their data. top.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
top.summary: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.
top.text: Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next. Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness. The findings, published in the journal Nature , challenge traditional assumptions about the relationship between consciousness and thinking. They could also provide new insights into how the brain processes memories and language, potentially leading to advances in technologies that help people communicate after neurological injuries. "Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," said Dr. Sameer Sheth, professor and Cullen Foundation Endowed chair of neurosurgery and a McNair Scholar at Baylor. "Even when patients are fully anesthetized, their brains continue to analyze the world around them." To investigate what happens inside the unconscious brain, Sheth, who is also a neurosurgeon at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, and his colleagues studied patients undergoing epilepsy surgery while under general anesthesia. These procedures offered an unusual opportunity to examine the hippocampus, a brain structure deeply involved in learning and memory. Located within the brain's temporal lobe, the hippocampus helps organize information and plays an important role in forming new memories. The researchers used advanced recording devices called Neuropixels probes to monitor electrical signals from hundreds of individual neurons in the hippocampus. These tiny probes can detect activity from many nerve cells simultaneously, providing a detailed picture of how groups of neurons respond to information. According to the researchers, this technology had not previously been used to investigate this particular brain region in this way. It allowed the team to examine how the hippocampus responds to sounds and language while patients are unconscious and unable to report what they experience. The first experiment involved playing a series of repeating tones, occasionally interrupted by a sound that differed from the others. Although the patients were under anesthesia, neurons in their hippocampus responded differently to the unexpected sounds. Even more surprisingly, the brain cells became better at distinguishing these unusual tones as the experiment continued. This improvement suggested that the hippocampus was showing signs of neural plasticity, the brain's ability to change its responses through experience. In other words, some of the basic processes associated with learning appeared to remain active even without conscious awareness. The researchers then tested whether the unconscious brain could handle something more complicated than simple sounds. They played short stories to the anesthetized patients while continuing to record activity from neurons in the hippocampus. The results revealed a surprising level of language processing. Distinct patterns of neural activity contained information about different categories of words, including nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This suggested that the hippocampus was responding to meaningful features of language rather than simply detecting that sounds were occurring. The researchers found that neural activity also carried information that could be used to predict upcoming words in a sentence. Even though the patients were unconscious, their brains appeared to anticipate how the language unfolding around them might continue. "The brain appears to anticipate what comes next in a story, even without conscious awareness," said Sheth, who is also Director of The Gordon and Mary Cain Pediatric Neurology Research Foundation Laboratories within the Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital. This ability is related to a process known as predictive coding. Rather than passively receiving information, the brain continually uses patterns and previous experience to anticipate what might happen next. When listening to someone speak, for example, the brain can use the words already heard to form expectations about what is likely to follow. Scientists have typically studied this kind of sophisticated prediction in people who are awake and paying attention. Finding evidence of it during general anesthesia suggests that at least some of the underlying neural processes can operate independently of conscious awareness. "This kind of predictive coding is something we associate with being awake and attentive, yet it's happening here in an unconscious state," said Dr. Benjamin Hayden, professor of neurosurgery at Baylor. The findings raise important questions about what consciousness actually contributes to the brain's ability to process information. Consciousness is generally associated with subjective awareness, including the experience of hearing, thinking, and understanding the world around us. Yet the study suggests that some neural processes involved in interpreting language and predicting future information can continue even when that awareness is absent. This does not necessarily mean that the anesthetized patients consciously understood the stories being played to them. Instead, it indicates that the brain can carry out surprisingly complex aspects of language processing without a person being aware of doing so. The distinction could help researchers better understand how consciousness emerges. One possibility is that awareness depends not simply on whether individual brain regions remain active, but on how information is coordinated and shared across larger networks of brain regions. Under this view, a structure such as the hippocampus might continue analyzing information even when the broader communication between brain regions needed for conscious experience is disrupted. A Surprising Connection Between the Brain and Artificial Intelligence The discovery also highlights an intriguing similarity between human brain activity and artificial intelligence (AI). Large language models, the technology behind many modern AI chatbots, generate text by using patterns learned from enormous amounts of language data to predict what should come next. The researchers observed a related predictive ability in the hippocampus, where neural signals reflected information about upcoming words even during unconsciousness. Although biological brains and AI models operate in fundamentally different ways, both can use patterns in language to anticipate future information. Studying these similarities may help scientists better understand how prediction works in natural and artificial systems. The findings could also have practical implications for brain-computer interfaces, which use signals recorded from the brain to communicate with external devices. One potential application involves speech prosthetics, technologies designed to help people communicate when injuries or neurological conditions have impaired their ability to speak. If scientists can reliably identify meaningful language signals in the brain, those signals might eventually be used to support communication technologies for patients who have lost speech abilities. "Can we use these signals to deploy and run a speech prosthetic for some of the parts of the brain that are damaged by stroke or injury? These are questions that we can now consider in relation to this part of the brain," said Dr. Vigi Katlowitz, first author and a neurosurgery resident with Baylor. Scientists Are Rethinking the Limits of the Unconscious Brain Despite the striking results, the researchers emphasize that several questions remain unanswered. top.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
top.summary: Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.
top.text: Forest soils are playing a surprisingly powerful role in removing methane from the atmosphere, and new findings suggest that certain effects of climate change could make them even better at it. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming, but microorganisms living in the soil can break it down before it builds up in the air. Scientists from the University of Göttingen and the Baden-Württemberg Forest Research Institute (FVA) analyzed the world's most comprehensive collection of long-term measurements of methane absorption by forest soils. Their findings revealed an unexpected trend: under certain climate conditions that could become more common in the future, forest soils can actually increase the amount of methane they remove from the atmosphere. The researchers examined measurements collected from 13 forest sites in southwestern Germany over periods of up to 24 years. On average, the amount of methane absorbed by the soils increased by approximately 3% annually. The researchers linked this rise to declining rainfall and warmer temperatures, which create conditions that make it easier for methane to enter the soil and be broken down by microorganisms. The findings, published in Agricultural and Forest Meteorology , challenge previous research suggesting that climate change is generally reducing the ability of forest soils to absorb methane. To understand how methane absorption changes over time, the researchers examined an extensive collection of soil gas measurements gathered through the FVA's long-running monitoring program. The measurements included soil gas profiles, which reveal the chemical composition of gases trapped in the soil at different depths. Every two weeks, researchers collected air samples through thin tubes installed beneath the ground and analyzed them in a laboratory. This repeated sampling allowed scientists to track changes in methane concentrations over many years. To confirm their findings, the team also used an independent measurement technique involving airtight chambers placed directly on the soil surface. By monitoring how gas concentrations changed inside these chambers, the researchers could determine whether the soil was absorbing methane and calculate how much was being removed. Combining these methods gave the scientists a detailed picture of methane uptake across the forest sites and how it responded to changing environmental conditions. Although methane absorption varied considerably between the 13 locations, a clear overall pattern emerged. Forest soils in southwestern Germany were particularly effective at removing methane from the atmosphere during periods of lower rainfall and higher temperatures. "Our long-term data shows that climate change does not necessarily have a negative impact on how much methane forest soils absorb. While the largest study to date from the US found a decline in methane uptake of up to 80 percent due to increasing rainfall, our significantly more comprehensive field study in south-western Germany found the opposite, " explains Professor Martin Maier at Göttingen University's Department of Crop Sciences, who led the study and was previously involved in the FVA's soil gas monitoring program. "We observed a significant long-term increase in methane uptake in the forest areas we studied." The explanation lies partly in how water moves through the ground. When soil becomes saturated with moisture, water fills many of the tiny spaces between soil particles, making it more difficult for gases to move through them. Drier soil contains more pores filled with air, allowing atmospheric methane to travel deeper into the ground. Once methane enters the soil, microorganisms use it as an energy source, breaking it down in the process. Rising temperatures can slightly accelerate this microbial activity, allowing the organisms to consume methane more quickly. Together, these two effects help explain why warmer temperatures and reduced rainfall were associated with greater methane absorption in the forests studied. The results offer a different perspective from several major international research reviews. These analyses, known as meta-analyses, combine findings from numerous individual studies to identify broader patterns. Many have concluded that methane absorption by forest soils is declining. However, the German study suggests that the relationship between climate change and methane uptake is more complicated than those overall trends indicate. While increasing rainfall can reduce methane absorption by limiting the movement of gas through soil, drier conditions can produce the opposite effect. The findings do not mean that climate change is beneficial for forests overall. Instead, they demonstrate that its effects on methane absorption can differ considerably depending on local temperatures, rainfall patterns, and soil conditions. The researchers emphasize that these regional differences make long-term monitoring especially important. Shorter studies or analyses that combine measurements from widely different environments may miss gradual changes that only become apparent after years of observation. "Our results make it clear that taking a series of measurements over many years and running monitoring programs are indispensable for assessing the real effects of climate change," says Maier. top.title: 210-million-year-old dinosaur discovery reveals a lost world in Africa
top.summary: A newly identified 210-million-year-old dinosaur from Zimbabwe is helping scientists uncover a surprisingly distinct prehistoric ecosystem. The discovery suggests that ancient climate differences may have separated dinosaur populations across southern Africa, leading to unique species that challenge previous assumptions about their evolution.
top.text: Africa boasts up to 25% of Earth’s animal and plant species . This diversity is driven by diverse habitats: harsh deserts, vast grasslands, dense forests, towering mountains, lush coastlines and teeming seas. It is also due to deep evolutionary roots, as many animal and plant groups originated here in the distant past. Paleontologists have been excavating this material for nearly two centuries . Africa is most famous for spectacular hominid fossils that reveal our own ancestry. However, the continent boasts many fabulous fossil finds, including those of the most familiar extinct animals – dinosaurs. The first African dinosaur fossils to be noted scientifically hailed from the Eastern Cape, South Africa and were described in the 1850s. Since then, the African dinosaur map has expanded, with rich fossil beds in South Africa, Lesotho, Tanzania, Egypt, Niger, Malawi, Madagascar and Morocco. Zimbabwe is an important part of the African dinosaur puzzle, with dinosaur bones reported since 1916 . As a specialist on early dinosaurs who has worked on similar material from China, the UK and Africa, I’ve been drawn to these Zimbabwean fossils to see what they reveal about the first stages of their evolution. Our latest addition to the Triassic zoo, Musango matusadonaensis , is a sauropodomorph dinosaur. (That’s the dinosaur subgroup that eventually gave rise to four-legged, long-necked giants like Diplodocus .) Its incomplete skeleton was found in the bank of the Nyamasango River close to Musango Island, as captured in the animal’s scientific name. Musango ’s anatomy shows us that it was bipedal (walking on its hind legs only), reached about 4.5 meters in length, and weighed 220kg. Growth marks in its bones reveal that it was a subadult when it died. Sadly, the skull wasn’t preserved, so its diet is unknown, but its close relatives were largely herbivorous (plant-eating). Our new work reveals something unexpected about Zimbabwean dinosaurs. They’re not simply an extension of better-known South African faunas but include an array of species unique to the region. We’re now trying to work out why these differences exist. We suspect that environmental conditions might be the key. Early fossil finds in Zimbabwe were overlooked by many scientists and it was not until the 1970s that they became more generally known . This was thanks to pioneering work by Zimbabwean paleontologists Geoffrey Bond and Michael Raath, who discovered abundant material in the hinterlands of Bulawayo (south-west Zimbabwe) and the lower Zambezi Valley (forming the border with Zambia). Most of these finds were identified as belonging to known species named from neighboring South Africa. Paleontological work in Zimbabwe stalled for a few decades. However, a band of devoted fossil hunters kept searching. One of them, Steve Edwards, a local safari camp manager, found new, productive sites on the shore of Lake Kariba, the artificial lake which forms most of the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia. News of the discoveries eventually reached Jonah Choiniere at the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg. Jonah, an expert on early dinosaurs, immediately recognized the importance of the material. He assembled an international team of South African, Zimbabwean and UK-based collaborators to explore them further. This was a major task, as the sites on Late Kariba’s shoreline are deep inside Matusadona National Park. Our solution was to use one of the Kariba houseboats as a mobile hotel and laboratory, so that we could prospect the shoreline. We mounted two expeditions, in 2017 and 2018. We have been cleaning and studying this material ever since. Both trips yielded a trove of material, collected from brick-red mudstones and sandstones that were laid down by ancient rivers around 210 million years ago, during the Late Triassic period (237-201 million years ago) . Geological evidence and plant fossils show that the Triassic landscape of Kariba was dry and dotted with stands of large conifer trees, with green corridors of vegetation following permanent watercourses. Sauropodomorphs are the most common Late Triassic dinosaurs. But what’s interesting about Musango and its relative Musankwa (which we described from the same beds in 2024) is that they are unique to Zimbabwe. We’d expected to find South African dinosaur species in these beds, given their similar age and geographic proximity, but surprisingly all the material we’ve collected so far has revealed animals that are distinct from those elsewhere. These Zimbabwean dinosaurs are not even the closest relatives of their South African neighbors. We’ve also found other fossil animals, including lungfish and aquatic reptiles called phytosaurs, which are rare or absent in South African sites. Following this, we’ve started to reappraise the historical dinosaur collections in Bulawayo. It appears that many of these fossils can’t be referred to South African species either, contrary to earlier assumptions. Then, as now, Zimbabwe was further north than South Africa and closer to the equator, so climatic differences might be responsible for these varied casts of characters (as climate is known to have a strong effect on the distributions of living animals). To probe this further, we’ll be going back to Kariba in search of more fossils. We’ll also collect more information on the exact ages and environments of these dinosaur-bearing rocks, to compare them more precisely with sites elsewhere. Although the significance of these dinosaurs is only just coming to light, Zimbabwe is already taking a greater role in shedding much needed light on early dinosaur evolution. top.title: Scientists discover a surprising danger in smaller cancer cells
top.summary: Scientists have discovered that unusually small cancer cells carrying extra chromosomes can be far more aggressive than larger ones, growing faster, spreading more readily, and resisting common treatments. The surprising finding could help explain why some tumors are especially dangerous and provide a new way to predict cancer outcomes.
top.text: Some cancers grow faster, spread more aggressively, and respond less effectively to treatment than others. Researchers at Virginia Tech are uncovering surprising reasons behind these differences, including how abnormal cancer cells recruit healthy tissue to support tumor growth and why the size of certain cancer cells could help predict their danger. The discoveries emerged from years of painstaking laboratory work, including the careful examination of tumors grown in mice. Graduate student Megan Sweet, who studies biological sciences at Virginia Tech, spends much of her time preparing extremely thin slices of tumor tissue. Working inside a refrigerated metal chamber, she carefully adjusts a mounted tumor, roughly the size of a pinkie fingernail, toward a sharp cutting blade. "It's all about fine-tuning and making sure it's going to be an even slice," said Sweet, who studies biological sciences. As the blade moves through the tissue, it produces a steady, rhythmic chopping sound. "This is the hardest and most time-consuming part," Sweet said. "But it's also kind of meditative." Each section is cut so thin that light can pass through it. Sweet carefully transfers the delicate tissue onto a glass slide, where selected cellular structures are stained to make them easier to distinguish under a powerful microscope. The process involves repeated rounds of cutting, staining, examining, and comparing samples. Although painstaking, this work is helping scientists piece together why certain tumors become much more dangerous than others. The Virginia Tech team has published findings that shed new light on how cancer develops and progresses. Their research was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , with additional findings published earlier this year in Cancer Research . Most healthy cells in the human body are diploid, meaning they contain two complete sets of chromosomes, with one inherited from each parent. Under normal conditions, these cells divide to produce new cells with the same chromosome arrangement. Occasionally, however, something goes wrong during division, leaving cells with an abnormal number of chromosomes. When these errors are passed on during subsequent cell divisions, they can accumulate over time. Such changes are one of the ways cancer can develop. For the past five years, Sweet and fellow graduate student Mat Bloomfield have worked with cell biologist Daniela Cimini to investigate cells carrying abnormal numbers of chromosomes, a common characteristic of cancer. To study the consequences of these abnormalities, Cimini's team manipulated diploid cancer cells so they would duplicate their chromosomes without completing cell division. The result was a type of cell known as a tetraploid cell, which contains four complete sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two. These cells are not limited to laboratory experiments. Tetraploid cells can also emerge during the development of human tumors, and their presence has been associated with cancer progression and poorer outcomes for patients. Scientists have long recognized that tetraploid cells can make tumors more aggressive. What remained unclear was exactly how they contributed to cancer growth. To investigate, Sweet and Bloomfield compared tumors that developed from ordinary diploid cancer cells with those formed from tetraploid cancer cells. As tumors grew in mice, the proportion of tetraploid cells actually decreased. Despite this decline, the tumors continued expanding rapidly and reached substantial sizes. The researchers discovered that tetraploid cancer cells were encouraging the recruitment of stromal cells, which are noncancerous connective tissue cells that help provide structural support. These additional cells appeared to create an environment that favored further tumor development. "The presence of even a small fraction of these tetraploid cells can promote the recruitment of extra non-cancerous cells that support further tumor progression," Sweet said. The finding revealed a previously unrecognized mechanism through which abnormal cancer cells can promote tumor growth, even when they account for only a small portion of the tumor. A separate investigation uncovered another unexpected connection between tetraploid cells and cancer aggressiveness. Bloomfield was initially examining the physical characteristics of tetraploid cells. After producing tetraploid cells from human cancer cells and establishing colonies derived from individual cells, he noticed that the resulting groups were not all the same size. Because tetraploid cells contain twice the usual number of chromosome sets, the researchers expected them to be approximately twice as large as diploid cells. Instead, some of the cells were 25 to 30 percent smaller than anticipated. Even more surprisingly, those smaller cells proved to be more capable of forming aggressive tumors than their larger counterparts. "The smaller clones are more aggressive," Bloomfield said. "They grow faster, are more invasive, and more tolerant of common anti-cancer and stress-inducing drugs." Further experiments in mice supported these observations. Tumors containing smaller tetraploid cells frequently grew more quickly than those containing larger ones. The pattern was not restricted to a single type of cancer. Researchers observed similar results in both colorectal and breast cancer cells, suggesting that the relationship between tetraploid cell size and tumor aggressiveness may extend across different cancers. The researchers next examined whether the same relationship could be found in human cancers. They analyzed information from the Cancer Genome Atlas, a large collection of detailed data from thousands of cancer patient samples. The results revealed that smaller tetraploid cells were associated with worse prognoses and lower survival rates across several cancer types. This suggests that measuring the size of these abnormal cells could provide valuable information about how aggressively a tumor might behave. "We already knew that tetraploidy can make cells more tumorigenic, but now we know that if you incorporate the size of the cells, it can be more predictive of tumorigenic potential," Cimini said. The findings add an important dimension to scientists' understanding of cancer. Abnormal chromosome numbers have long been linked to dangerous tumor behavior, but the new research indicates that cell size may offer additional clues about a cancer's potential to grow and spread. The team now plans to investigate the biological mechanisms responsible for these effects in greater detail while continuing to examine human cancer data. For Sweet, that means more hours at the laboratory bench, carefully cutting and analyzing tiny sections of tumor tissue in the search for answers to one of cancer biology's most important questions. top.title: Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
top.summary: Ice baths, massages, compression garments, and recovery supplements promise faster muscle recovery, but research suggests their benefits are often overstated, and some techniques may even undermine long-term gains. Scientists say the most effective recovery methods are far simpler and cheaper: getting enough sleep, eating well, and giving muscles time to rebuild.
top.text: Finishing a tough workout always feels good. That is, until a few hours later when those uncomfortable muscle aches start setting in. This discomfort can linger for days – making easy, everyday tasks a challenge. In search of relief, some recreational gym-goers are adopting the kind of recovery techniques once reserved for elite athletes. Social media and professional sport have helped popularize everything from ice baths and compression garments to massage and recovery supplements. While many of these products promise faster recovery, reduced soreness and improved performance, the science is often more nuanced. Few recovery strategies have received as much attention as ice baths . This involves immersing oneself in water that is below 15°C to boost recovery. But the evidence for this benefit is mixed. Ice baths help ease inflammation, which research suggests can reduce muscle soreness and help athletes recover muscle function more effectively in a 24-hour period. But there’s a catch. While inflammation causes soreness, it also triggers adaptations that build muscle . Dampening this response with ice baths may limit some of the long-term benefits of training – particularly if they’re used regularly. When it comes to ice baths, side-stepping short-term pain may sacrifice long-term gains. It’s best to only use them when rapid recovery is vital. Compression garments are commonly worn after exercise to speed recovery . The idea is that the external pressure they apply supports circulation, enhances blood flow to the muscles, and reduces swelling. But while compression garments might make you think they’re helping as they reduce soreness, evidence showing they actually improve muscle recovery is generally less convincing . A study from 2022 put them to the test. One group was given compression garments; the other group was given a placebo tablet that they were told was equally as effective as compression. The compression garments were shown to improve circulation and muscle blood flow, while the placebo had no effect on these measures. This suggests the effects of compression garments on recovery are physiological and aren’t simply due to expectation or perception. However, whether these changes meaningfully improve performance is less clear. Although emerging evidence suggests compression garments genuinely affect some markers of recovery, this is unlikely to directly restore muscle function . So, compression garments may mainly help because they make you feel better recovered. Massage is one of the few recovery interventions with relatively consistent scientific support . It can reduce soreness and improve perceived recovery after exercise. It’s not currently clear what mechanisms actually trigger the recovery benefits of massage . But it could be due to the fact that massage reduces muscle stiffness, improves circulation and boosts relaxation. But although athletes feel less sore and perceptions of recovery are improved after a massage, objective measures of performance and muscle function are modest and inconsistent . Massage might ease the discomfort of training, but don’t expect miraculous performance restoration. The nutrition supplement market is a big business, with hundreds of brightly coloured recovery drinks and capsules promising reduced soreness and faster recovery. But not all supplements are created equal. Some appear to confer small benefits, while some come with hype that science doesn’t back up. Whey protein, for instance, is a well-researched supplement. Rich in amino acids (the building blocks of protein), it stimulates muscle protein synthesis – the process which helps your muscles grow. Whey protein is shown to have small-to-moderate benefits for muscle recovery – but evidence that it can alleviate soreness is inconsistent . Branch chain amino acids (BCAAs) are widely-used supplements that typically contain a mixture of the amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine. BCAAs are popular because it’s believed the leucine they contain switches on protein synthesis . Yet despite their popularity, BCAAs appear less effective than complete protein sources for muscle recovery. This is because muscle repair requires all essential amino acids – not just the ones found in BCAAs. Food sources such as chicken, beef, salmon and tofu contain all the essential amino acids. Tart cherry juice is a relatively new supplement in the fitness world. It’s rich in polyphenols – plant compounds that are said to have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant (reducing or preventing cell damage) effects. It’s for these reasons that tart cherry juice is thought to help reduce muscle damage and soreness . Although this is still an emerging area of research, evidence suggests these compounds have small-to-moderate effects on reducing soreness after workouts, and may also help restore muscular strength and power. Omega-3 (fish oil) supplements are often championed as a way to reduce inflammation and accelerate recovery after exercise. While some research suggests they can modestly reduce muscle soreness and help preserve muscle function after strenuous exercise, results are far from consistent . As such, omega-3 supplements are unlikely to vastly improve recovery. Importantly, all of these nutrients can be obtained from a healthy, balanced diet. Science also shows that it’s better to get these nutrients from whole foods over expensive supplements, as whole foods provide other important nutrients that may interact synergistically to support health. Popular recovery techniques might have small benefits for reducing feelings of soreness, but they don’t actually tend to restore muscle function all that much. Instead, the strongest evidence for good recovery comes from the basics: So, perhaps the biggest lesson here is that recovery cannot be bottled and sold. Materials provided by The Conversation . top.title: Legal encounters may offer overlooked opportunities for suicide prevention, analysis suggests
top.summary: Picture a forlorn man walking into a lawyer's office after his marriage has collapsed. The bank is threatening foreclosure, and his finances are in tatters. His problems may be legal on paper, but in person they can look far more complicated: panic, shame or the numb resignation of someone who can no longer imagine a way out. He did not come for counseling, and his lawyer is not a therapist. Still, the attorney may be sitting beside him at the worst moment of his life—with a chance to help before despair slides into tragedy.

top.title: Implicit language hierarchies in English-taught programs create ambivalent positions for multilingual students
top.summary: A new study by Miki Shibata, a professor at Hiroshima University's Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, reveals a paradox in Japan's English-medium higher education: Official English instruction coexists with local peer expectations that drive classroom interactions back into Japanese.

top.title: Petting your dog may help your body handle the next stressful situation better
top.summary: Coming home to a four-legged furry friend wagging their tail can ease the stress accumulated throughout the day. Since time immemorial, humans have found comfort in petting their dogs. A large body of research acknowledges the well-being benefits of pet ownership, but the mechanisms that drive those benefits remain murky.

top.title: Prenatal iron deficiency leaves lasting changes in the developing brain
top.summary: During the first weeks of pregnancy, developing cells are already laying the foundation for the brain. Iron plays a major role in the organization and shaping of cells during this stage of gestation. Epidemiological studies suggest that mothers with low iron levels during the first trimester of pregnancy have a higher risk of giving birth to a child who develops cognitive impairments like autism, ADHD and learning disabilities.
